title: CDC Staff Cuts Leave US Struggling to Contain Largest Cyclospora Outbreak on Record
excerpt: The parasitic disease lab shrank from 11 people to three after USAID funding was axed, slowing the federal response as more than 7,000 Americans fell ill from contaminated lettuce.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Over 7,000 cyclospora cases reported across 34 states, with Michigan alone accounting for over 5,000.
  • CDC's parasitic diseases lab reduced from 11 to 3 staff due to budget cuts, crippling outbreak response.
  • Outbreak linked to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico, affecting Taco Bell in five states.
  • CDC's public notification about the outbreak lagged by two weeks, marking the worst reporting gap in 15 years.

  • More than 7,000 cyclospora cases have been confirmed or are under investigation across 34 states, with Michigan alone reporting over 5,000 infections — potentially the largest cyclospora outbreak in US history.
  • The CDC's parasitic diseases lab shrank from 11 specialists to three after Trump administration budget cuts eliminated nearly $30 million in USAID-linked funding; the former lab director resigned and warned of this exact scenario.
  • FDA traceback identified Taylor Farms de Mexico's shredded iceberg lettuce, served at Taco Bell locations in five Midwestern states, as the outbreak source; the company has recalled lettuce distributed to 27 states.
  • The CDC took until July 14 to publicly notify Americans about the outbreak — two weeks after Michigan issued its own warning — a reporting lag insiders call unprecedented in 15 years.

The federal government's ability to respond to a surging cyclospora outbreak has been severely hampered by staff losses and funding cuts at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, according to former officials and sources familiar with the investigation.

More than 7,000 cases of cyclosporiasis — an intestinal infection caused by a microscopic parasite typically spread through contaminated fresh produce — have been confirmed or are under investigation in 34 states, according to the CDC. At least 141 people have been hospitalized, though no deaths have been reported. Michigan has been hit hardest, with more than 5,000 cases, compared to the 40 to 50 it typically sees annually.

A Gutted Team

Dr. Joel Barratt, who led the CDC's federal lab responsible for identifying parasitic outbreaks, watched his 11-person team dwindle to three as the Trump administration imposed hiring freezes and cut budgets through 2025. He resigned in September after warning superiors that the staffing collapse would cripple the agency's ability to respond to future outbreaks.

"The response is being hampered by the loss of specialized staff and the loss of hands-on-deck needed to identify the source of the outbreaks."

— Dr. Joel Barratt, former CDC parasitic diseases lab director

The Division of Parasitic Diseases and Malaria lost nearly $29 million when the Trump administration dismantled USAID. While the White House characterized the lost funds as supporting overseas programs, former officials told CNN that the money also paid for shared lab equipment and staff who could be mobilized during domestic outbreaks. The CDC lost roughly a quarter of its workforce in 2025 through reduction-in-force cuts.

"The people who've led this work last year and maybe the 10 or 20 years before that no longer work at the agency," a source familiar with the CDC's outbreak investigation told CNN. "A lot of that knowledge is lost."

Tracing the Source

Federal investigators on July 16 announced that the Midwestern cluster was linked to shredded iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell restaurants in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and West Virginia. The FDA's traceback investigation converged on a single supplier: Taylor Farms de Mexico, based in Guanajuato.

On July 17, Taylor Farms de Mexico voluntarily recalled all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico, affecting products distributed from June 29 through July 16 across 27 states. Taco Bell said it had removed all affected lettuce from its restaurants. Walmart also pulled Marketside-brand iceberg salad and shredded lettuce products. Sysco, the nation's largest food distributor, halted all sales of Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce from Mexico.

In a twist, the FDA said Sunday that an initial positive test for cyclospora on a Taylor Farms lettuce sample was actually a false positive. The agency said no product samples have produced a confirmed positive result, though the epidemiological link between Taco Bell lettuce and the infections remains firm.

Surveillance Gaps

The outbreak has exposed deeper cracks in America's food safety infrastructure. In July 2025, the CDC's FoodNet surveillance program — a collaboration between the CDC, USDA, FDA, and 10 state health departments — stopped tracking cyclospora and five other pathogens due to funding cuts, narrowing its focus to only salmonella and a dangerous strain of E. coli.

"If you want to make foodborne disease go away, then don't look for foodborne disease," J. Glenn Morris of the University of Florida, who helped create FoodNet in the 1990s, told NBC News.

The CDC did not notify the public or healthcare providers about the outbreak until July 14 — two weeks after Michigan issued its own warning. Meanwhile, the CDC's confirmed case count of 1,645 lagged far behind states' own tallies, a reporting gap insiders described as the worst in 15 years.

"This outbreak deserves a hot wash, or a major review, because there were so many things we could learn from this that went wrong."

— Dr. Michael Osterholm, Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy, University of Minnesota

What Consumers Should Know

Health officials advise consumers to discard any recalled Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce products immediately. Symptoms of cyclosporiasis include watery diarrhea, cramping, and bloating that can persist for weeks; the incubation period ranges from two days to two weeks. Cooking leafy greens to 158°F or above kills the parasite, while washing alone is not effective at eliminating it, according to Rutgers University food scientist Donald Schaffner.

The standard treatment is the antibiotic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim), taken twice daily for seven to 10 days. Cases typically rise through August, and officials expect the count to climb further before the outbreak is contained.
